source: Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = W/Δt = Fv.
Students mix up power with energy, or use P = Fv with a force that isn't along the velocity.
Power measured how fast energy is transferred. Two students climbing the same stairs do the same Work by a Constant Force, but the one who runs delivers it faster.
Power is the rate of energy transfer: $P = \dfrac{W}{\Delta t}$, in watts ($1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$). For a force pushing along the velocity, $P = Fv$.

Work divided by time is a rate, like speed is distance divided by time. If a force $F$ pushes along the motion, in a short time $\Delta t$ the object moves $v\Delta t$, so the work is $Fv\Delta t$ and the power is $Fv$. That's why a car's engine works hardest at highway speed: drag is large and so is $v$.
Energy delivered against time: 600 W for 10 s, a rest, then 900 W.
A $60\ \text{kg}$ hiker climbs $12\ \text{m}$ of stairs in $15\ \text{s}$. What power does the climb take?
A car cruises at $25\ \text{m/s}$ against $600\ \text{N}$ of drag and rolling friction. What power reaches the wheels?
At steady speed the forward force equals $600\ \text{N}$, along the velocity.
A $1{,}500\ \text{W}$ hair dryer runs for $5$ minutes. How much energy does it use?
An electric bill counts energy in kilowatt-hours. How many joules is $1\ \text{kW}\cdot\text{h}$?
$1\ \text{kW}\cdot\text{h} = 1000 \times 3600 = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$, an amount of energy, not a power.

Mixing up power with energy (watts are joules per second; a kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy), or using $P = Fv$ with a force that isn't along the velocity. Check the units: power must come out in J/s. If the force is at an angle, use only its part along the velocity: $P = Fv\cos\theta$.
